summary:
Greenland is a self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark, with its own parliament and courts handling domestic affairs. Danish legislation on marriage and on official identity documents has been adopted and applies here, so the legal position a visitor encounters on those questions follows the Danish framework as received in Greenland.

The sources record no criminal penalty for same-sex relations. Since 2010 Article 100 of the Criminal Code has prohibited speech that may deprive, threaten or demean people on the basis of sexual orientation among other protected categories, and the Code provides penalty enhancement for hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation. No reported cases of prosecution under these provisions appear in the inventory.

Same-sex marriage has been in effect since 1 April 2016, under legislation adopted from the Danish bill that was passed unanimously twice after an earlier version lapsed with Danish elections. It replaced the registered partnership regime (nalunaarsukkamik inooqatigiinneq) that had run from 1 July 1996 until that date. The bishop of the established church supported the marriage law.

Trans visitors can change the sex designation on official identity documents through a Greenlandic procedure introduced by decree in 2016. Legal sex change rests on self-determination: no sex reassignment surgery, hormone therapy, sterilisation or medical diagnosis is required. Applicants must be over 18 and state that they want their documentation changed, then observe a six-month reflection period before the request is confirmed. Greenlandic passports are issued with an "X" sex descriptor as well as male and female, which allows a marker consistent with a non-binary presentation at the border.

Greenland's parliament passed a Law on Equal Treatment and Anti-Discrimination in May 2024, in force from 1 July 2024, prohibiting discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and gender characteristics among others. The law establishes an Equal Treatment Board to handle discrimination complaints and an Equality Council to promote non-discrimination. The state-funded Human Rights Council of Greenland works closely with the Danish Institute for Human Rights.

The recorded social climate is quiet and non-violent. Reporting from May 2015 describes gay life as low-key, integrated and free of hostility, with a modest Pride march held in Nuuk since 2010; the first Pride parade took place there on 15 May 2010 and drew about 1,000 people. The population is small and scattered, so there is virtually no organised scene, though a handful of nightclubs and bars in Nuuk draw a mixed gay and straight crowd.
tangentialFactors:
The 1996 registered partnership law passed with virtually no public debate, and the 2016 marriage bill drew support from the bishop of the established church. Both points indicate that legislative change on same-sex relationships has not been a site of open political conflict in Greenland.

The comparative position is that much of the trans-specific framework arrived by adoption from Denmark rather than by domestic drafting, while the 2016 document-change decree and the 2024 equal treatment law are Greenlandic instruments. Visitors should therefore expect Danish-derived rules on status documents and a locally administered complaints machinery for discrimination.

Public visibility has grown steadily rather than through confrontation: a Pride march from 2010, a national LGBT association founded in 2014, and a statutory equal treatment body in 2024. Nothing in the inventory records protests, rollbacks or counter-mobilisation directed at LGBT people.
localsOnly:
Greenlandic Broadcasting reported in August 2014 that a new national association, LGBT Qaamaneq, had been founded for lesbians, gays, bisexuals and transgender people. It works for political, cultural and social equality and is open to family members, friends and colleagues as supporters.

Residents discriminated against on the protected grounds can bring complaints to the Equal Treatment Board established by the Law on Equal Treatment and Anti-Discrimination, in force 1 July 2024, and the Equality Council is mandated to promote non-discrimination. The state-funded Human Rights Council of Greenland cooperates with the Danish Institute for Human Rights on the promotion and protection of human rights.

Residents changing the sex designation on their identity documents follow the 2016 decree procedure: an application by a person over 18 stating the wish to change their documentation, a six-month reflection period, and confirmation, with no medical requirements attached.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no reporting on how the hate-speech and hate-crime provisions of Article 100 have been applied, so their enforcement record is unresolved. No trans-specific incident data, including any assault or police-responded violence in Greenland, is sourced here.

Entry and visa requirements, border screening practices, and whether gender markers are checked against passports at Nuuk airport are not covered by the sources and remain not sourced. The operation of the six-month reflection period in practice, and current processing times for document changes, are likewise not sourced.

It is unresolved from these sources whether the Equal Treatment Board has issued decisions concerning gender identity or gender expression since 1 July 2024, and whether any facility or bathroom rules specific to trans people are set nationally or left to individual institutions.
